assessment.nobel_worthiness: A foundational and unusually influential account of social preferences that reshaped experimental, labour, contract and behavioural economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr, Falk and Schmidt are central, complementary contributors to the experimental and theoretical programme.
assessment.maturity: The central findings and their implications have been tested extensively across settings over several decades.
uncertainties: The literature contains important heterogeneity across populations and institutional environments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Experimental markets and behavioural game theory made controlled evidence central to the study of strategic economic behaviour.
assessment.attribution: Plott, Camerer and Holt represent distinct foundational contributions to market experiments, behavioural games and experimental method.
assessment.maturity: The programme is longstanding, highly generative and supported by a large accumulated experimental record.
uncertainties: The candidate formulation encompasses several related strands and cannot fully recognize all foundational experimental economists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification provided a principled alternative to unwarranted point identification and materially improved empirical credibility.
assessment.attribution: Manski supplied the foundational framework, while Tamer and Molinari made major contributions to moment inequalities and applied inference.
assessment.maturity: The methods are well established and broadly used where assumptions are transparently consequential.
uncertainties: Its impact is methodologically deep but less visible outside empirical econometrics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative-data research transformed the measurement and interpretation of intergenerational mobility and place-based opportunity.
assessment.attribution: Chetty and Hendren are especially central to the data and mobility programme, with Katz a major formative collaborator.
assessment.maturity: The measurement framework has produced a substantial, influential body of replicated and policy-relevant work.
uncertainties: The work has several indispensable collaborators, including John N. Friedman, beyond the three available prize slots.
Interpretation of descriptive mobility patterns as causal policy guidance remains contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection became a core framework for understanding trade patterns, productivity and welfare from trade.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's framework is central, with Helpman and Redding making major linked theoretical and empirical contributions.
assessment.maturity: The approach has endured as a workhorse model and has generated extensive empirical testing.
uncertainties: Quantitative welfare conclusions remain sensitive to modelling and trade-cost assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work supplied persuasive empirical frameworks for understanding technology, trade shocks and changing labour-market inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson form a coherent group responsible for seminal evidence on tasks, polarization and local trade exposure.
assessment.maturity: The research has changed labour-economics practice and stimulated extensive follow-up evidence.
uncertainties: The size and distribution of trade-shock effects can depend on exposure definitions and general-equilibrium interpretation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical and empirical study of insurance selection has substantially improved understanding of insurance-market design and welfare.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav and Salanie each made major contributions linking selection theory to credible measurement.
assessment.maturity: The approach is mature, influential across health and other insurance markets, and closely connected to policy design.
uncertainties: Selection and welfare estimates can remain context-specific and dependent on institutional detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence studies made discrimination in labour markets directly measurable and placed experimental evidence at the centre of a major policy question.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan produced landmark field-experimental evidence, while Charles made important related contributions to the economics of racial inequality.
assessment.maturity: The research design has been widely replicated, extended and incorporated into labour-market research and policy debate.
uncertainties: Audit outcomes identify discrimination at particular margins and do not alone measure its full aggregate or dynamic consequences.
